On Reuse Beyond Simondon Giovanni Carrozzini Résumé L’article analyse de manière critique le statut de l’obsolescence des objets techniques dans le contexte de la société contemporaine de consommation, en prenant pour axe théorique central la philosophie de la technique de Gilbert Simondon. L’auteur soutient que l’obsolescence n’est pas principalement un phénomène technique, mais un phénomène social, symbolique et économique, produit par les dynamiques du marché, par la publicité et par la logique de l’innovation permanente, qui dissocient l’objet de sa durabilité structurelle. À partir de ce constat, le texte propose la réutilisation comme un geste technique, éthique et politique, distinct de la simple pratique du recyclage ou de la restauration. Réutiliser signifie réinvestir l’objet de nouveaux schèmes fonctionnels, inaugurant ainsi un nouveau cycle inventif qui préserve le noyau technique de l’artefact et réinscrit l’humain dans la relation à la technique. Cette pratique est présentée comme une forme de résistance à la déshumanisation de la consommation et à la réduction des objets à de simples marchandises jetables. L’article examine également les liens entre réutilisation, écoconception et économie circulaire, en soulignant la nécessité de repenser le design à partir de la durabilité, de la démontabilité et de l’ouverture fonctionnelle des objets. Des exemples issus du design, de l’art contemporain et de pratiques éducatives illustrent la manière dont des objets obsolètes peuvent acquérir de nouvelles fonctions, des valeurs symboliques et une pertinence sociale renouvelée. Enfin, le texte défend l’idée que la culture de la réutilisation implique une transformation plus large de la société, fondée sur des principes de responsabilité, d’imagination technique et d’éducation, capables de promouvoir une relation plus éthique, durable et solidaire aux objets techniques. Mots-clés : Obsolescence des objets techniques; Philosophie de la technique; Réutilisation; Économie circulaire; Design durable. Aion Journal of Philosophy and Science 3, 2026 CONTACT: Giovanni Carrozzini, Università del Salento, giovannicarrozzini@gmail.com

Giovanni Carrozzini 19 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 Abstract The article critically examines the status of the obsolescence of technical objects within the context of contemporary consumer society, taking Gilbert Simondon’s philosophy of technology as its central theoretical framework. The author argues that obsolescence is not primarily a technical phenomenon, but rather a social, symbolic, and economic one, produced by market dynamics, advertising, and the logic of permanent innovation, which detach the object from its structural durability. On the basis of this observation, the text proposes reuse as a technical, ethical, and political gesture, distinct from the simple practices of recycling or restoration. To reuse means to reinvest the object with new functional schemata, thereby inaugurating a new inventive cycle that preserves the technical core of the artefact and reinscribes the human within the relationship to technology. This practice is presented as a form of resistance to the dehumanization of consumption and to the reduction of objects to mere disposable commodities. The article further examines the connections between reuse, ecodesign, and the circular economy, emphasizing the need to rethink design in terms of durability, dismantlability, and the functional openness of objects. Examples drawn from design, contemporary art, and educational practices illustrate how obsolete objects can acquire new functions, symbolic values, and renewed social relevance. Finally, the text argues that a culture of reuse entails a broader transformation of society, grounded in principles of responsibility, technical imagination, and education, capable of fostering a more ethical, sustainable, and solidaristic relationship with technical objects. Keywords: Obsolescence of technical objects; Philosophy of technology; Reuse; Circular economy; Sustainable design. Is the Object Obsolescent ? 20 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 Je suis allé au marché à la ferraille Et j’ai acheté des chaines De lourdes chaines Pour toi mon amour 2 Jacques Prévert, Pour toi mon amour [1946] 1. Reinventing a Technical Object. The current world demands a reversal of our attitude toward objects. Consumption and the frenzy for novelty have led us to become true executioners of objects. We must save them at all costs—and not only for environmental reasons. To save them from the fate that reduces them to waste, we must give them the chance to extend their life—that is, recycle or restore them—or to have another life, that is, reuse them, which is perhaps the best gesture to oppose the constraints of the global market. Now, the reuse of technical objects is not merely an ecological requirement; it is above all a question of a purely technical nature, as Gilbert Simondon—the only philosopher of the 20th century who analyzed techniques as such—noted. In 1983, during a very dense interview with Anita Ketchichian for the journal Esprit, the philosopher from Saint-Étienne observed: “[t]he true technology is a reinvention. […]. We must preserve the material of the past because it represents a possibility of revival, and not only to constitute an archaeology. […]. Techniques are never completely and forever in the past. They contain an inalienable schematic power that deserves to be preserved and safeguarded.” 3 Thus, reuse, as reinvention, is strictly linked to the obsolescence of objects, and the idea of technical obsolescence fits into Simondon’s overall perspective regarding the evolutionary process of objects; he indeed writes on this subject: “one must consider as an aspect of consumption the fact of social obsolescence: an automobile, just like a hat, is out of fashion before it is worn out or technically outdated.”4 Reused objects—that is, objects that have already passed their phase of obsolescence— trigger a new inventive cycle, and invention, for Simondon, is precisely the human part of the object that must be recognized, protected, and ‘saved,’ to oppose “the loss of passion of the individual toward the object, a kind of depersonalization of the human/object relationship.” 5 Simondon himself was a practitioner of reuse, if it is true that, as Jean-Marie Charpentier recounts, in Poitiers, in his Psychology Laboratory, he had used decommissioned American radars to make oscilloscopes 6. 2 “I went to the scrap market / And I bought chains / Heavy chains / For you, my love” (T.N.) 3 Simondon, G., 1983, “Sauver l’objet technique”, in Sur la technique (1953–1983), J.-Y. Giovanni Carrozzini 21 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 To return to the general question, we can say that to reuse is not only to restore or recycle an object; it is rather to reinvent it, to give it a chance to begin a new adventure, free in relation to its inventor—an adventure that is quasi-autonomous, but not independent. A requirement, that of reuse, is becoming ever more urgent in the contemporary world, since it is true that today “the entire production/consumption mechanism inexorably aims to configure the product in a one-way sense, for a programmed use, oriented toward ever-increasing thresholds of innovation, but not always necessary, and in fact functionalized by the logics of profit and the market.” 7 Now, the “art” of reusing objects is not a skill acquired by digital natives; as Pulvirenti observes on this point: “‘We’ll keep this… it might come in handy!’ That was the philosophy of our grandmothers, who never threw anything away because maybe, one day, that thing could become useful again.” 8 But it must be added that the reuse of objects varies according to cultures and geographic areas. Reuse can indeed arise from the need to address the problem of accumulation, as is the case in developed countries, but it can also arise for other reasons, “in developing countries [where] the problem is linked to the lack of means, the lack of goods and advanced resources, rather than to their overabundance as in rich countries.” 9 The question that arises in any case regarding the reuse of objects is precisely: what is a technical object to be reused? The answer comes to us from Simondon: an object is not only the coherent technical organism, but also its components—the elements— and its organizational ensembles—the systems. Reuse therefore demands from us a true rediscovery of technical thought, softened by the constraints of the global, globalized, and globalizing economy—that is, the economy that dominates a society that “scraps, throws away, eliminates, forgets, loses, recycles everything that is no longer new, no longer efficient, no longer perfect and youthful, lucid and taut, whole and integrable into a system.” 10 As Simondon writes: “[T]he object, as an object of use, is subject to a process of progressive degradation through wear, corrosion, deformation. In certain objects, such as a microscope, this process is almost inoperative if the object is well maintained. However, a certain halo effect spreads, starting from objects that deteriorate, to all technical objects, and leads one to think that they lose their quality of use over time. […] [O]ne can consider this process of invisible but presumable degradation as one of the bases of the depreciation of objects of use over time.” 11 7 Pagliero, A., 2007, Redesign. Is the Object Obsolescent ? 22 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 2. Is the Object Obsolescent? However, before analyzing the civility of reuse, to use Guido Viale’s expression, we must study the process that contributes to the obsolescence of an object. It is true, as Viale notes, that: “the current productive world, in fact, because of and according to its ever-increasing implications, conditions the existence of objects to a kind of relativity that is all the more significant as their functional and meaningful complexity is high, and more variable as their placement is taken within the structures of the market.” 12 From this point of view, advertising and fashion are two determining factors: they contribute to the arrival of the ‘new’ and the eclipse of the ‘old,’ independently of authentically technical evaluation criteria. So here we are talking about the fashion for the ‘new’ and not about that which rediscovers the old object—the ‘retro’ style that Simondon tells us in 1983 reinserts the object “into the present.” 13 Now, the technical object possesses at least three types of values: exchange or economic value, technical or structural value, and symbolic value. Advertising and fashion work mainly on the first and the third, and—as Simondon puts it—thus contribute to the exaltation of the over-historicity of the object, that is, to its overdetermination “as a psycho-social symbol” 14; over-historicity is not neutral with respect to the object, because it “creates barriers, of which an example can be given in the fact that an automobile goes out of fashion faster than it wears out.” 15 Fashion and advertising focus on the object’s contemporaneity; on the contrary, we should focus, technically, on its durability and permanence, because it is true that “the life cycle of an object could be as long as the technical, functional, and representative conditions that characterize it remain and endure.” 16 On this point, it is also true that Simondon had thought of a new advertising strategy respectful of the technical identity of objects: “at the level of a true advertising strategy, the handling of motivations gives way to a positive task of information intended to form archetypes from which cognitive structures will emerge. […] [T]he point is not to sell, but to invent the object that will be manufactured so that it can be sold without advertising.” 17 But it is his dreamer’s spirit that suggests this conclusion: for advertising, from its birth to today, things have worked very differently. Returning now to durability, it is the principle of ecodesign, whose promises aim “not only at the use of recycled materials in their production and at saving resources and energy during their manufacture, use, and handling; but also all operations of identifying 12 Viale, G., 2011, La civiltà del riuso. Giovanni Carrozzini 23 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 and reassembling disused products and the recovery and recycling of their materials and components” 18; more generally, it is “the imaginative capacity to seek alternative systems, technologies, and strategies.” 19 To return to the question we asked ourselves: how does an object become obsolescent? Viale suggests on this point that: “the entry of a thing into the world of the used is a complex passage, composed of at least two distinct moments; the decision to get rid of an object because it no longer serves, we no longer like it, we no longer want it, or we can no longer stand it; and the operation of removing it, giving it away, consigning it, or taking it away; because it may serve or please someone other than the one who used it. 20 It is the moment when we part with an object that its “meaning” is revealed: its obsolescence as an everyday object of use gives way to its persistence in the realm of existence, of affectivity. It is then that the necessity arises to think about the destiny of the object as such, once it has lost its immediate utility but not yet its existence. It is indeed true that an object, as an object, “can suggest an idea of material permanence and continuity of uses and meanings; in every domain, each material thing presents aspects of permanence, in constant contradiction with the impulses of continual innovation and transformation typical of contemporary reality; reasons and motives of affection, representativeness, and memory make this same idea of permanence appear as a kind of added value to that already implicit, which is contained in its material structure and in its capacities to endure beyond the conventional limits often imposed by contextual circumstances.” 21 The object thus becomes the protagonist of a series of possible human actions: inventory, give, throw away, sell, or reuse. Now, reuse is, according to Viale, “the second life of the thing,” 22 and therefore, in this series of possible actions, reuse is the only truly technical act: it is a gesture made to the object for the object, which consists in reinventing it, as we have already said. But the universe of reuse is a complex universe. There are at least three types of possible reuse: “a) the reuse of an artifact for the same function, by working to restore it. b) the reuse of an artifact for similar functions by making the necessary modifications. c) the recovery of the components of an artifact to reproduce a similar type or another type, depending on the shape and availability of the parts.” 23 In any case, reuse involves a first common moment, which I would dare to define as an epoché with respect to its over-historicity: that is, the detachment from the affective-emotional meaning it may have previously 18 Viale, G., 2011, La civiltà del riuso. But a society that reinvents, a technical society—that is, a society that thinks and works in a technical way—is above all a human society, all too human. The society of reuse is a transindividual society, where the transindividual can be conceived as the foundation of solidarity: “a solidary and convivial society is also a human consortium where things ‘ask’ to be used by many people, to have a new master if they have lost the previous one.” 24 This society would be founded on a vaguely Kantian imperative, adapted in Simondon’s manner: “always treat the object as an end, never as a means,” or again, “do not do to the object what you would not want done to you,” thus opposing the… “the dis-humanity that loses the sense of the past, of roots, the archetypal bond with the object, the sense of the beauty of a gaze, of a face, of a figure marked by life […] or lowered and immersed in its thoughts […]; the system that revolves around an alienating, frantic, exaggerated consumerism and eyes maddened by the money-god is killing the soul, is erasing the time to observe, to appreciate, to think, to meditate—the time of the essence of man.” 25 It is indeed true that “the overcoming of the utilitarian approach in the cognitive domain—and of the utilitarian ethics that is consubstantial with it—is a revolution of thought and conduct that removes man from his position as center and master of the world, to place works and activities within broader cycles of which they represent a segment, but which it is dangerous to interrupt.” 26 This approach is therefore driven not only by the need to rethink the object, but above all by the need to redesign society. If, as Pagliero observes, renewal and innovation are the watchwords of the contemporary product industry and “the frenzy for novelty (…) is a true monstrosity,” 27 as Simondon asserts, the philosophy of Redesign primarily raises environmental questions: “the principles and philosophies of Redesign extend their rationale by referring to environmental issues, as hypotheses for reconfiguring products and services based on durability and compatibility.” 28 This is precisely a reversal of the constraints of capital, which transform us into serial destroyers who unleash their repressed rage on their objects, against this “kind of violence, of disorder,” 29 as Simondon precisely says: for example, in the case of truck shows where vehicles crash into each other like gladiators in the arena—“this fight against 24 Viale, G., 2011, La civiltà del riuso. If all our sufferings came from technical objects, it would suffice to drown them in the sea, after ritually charging them with our faults.” 30 It is indeed true that—as Pagliero says, directly quoting Simondon: “in the contemporary world, the meaning of a product is determined by reasons external to its nature as a ‘technical object,’ according to Simondon’s definitions; which refer to those forms, structures, and functions that define its technological-material status; in other words, its logical meaning, independently of the reasons for hypertrophies of production and market.” 31 3. Throw away objects? Now, before addressing reuse as such, it is necessary to analyze it in relation to another possible action toward the object as an obsolete component: namely, the action of “throwing away.” The technical culture of reuse does not imply that everything must or can be saved: “there are sets of objects […] which, due to their technical and constructive structure, can be difficult to rehabilitate, as is the case for those that exhaust themselves in the exercise of their function: for example, a battery, a light bulb, or a garment after a certain limit of use.” 32 We must therefore learn to throw away. But what should be done with all the discarded objects that can be reused? The first way to reuse discarded objects is to look for them in the trash, in large landfills. There are people who have made this activity a way to save objects. But it is a rather uninventive way: it is limited to prolonging the life of objects without reinventing them, except in cases where waste becomes components for the creation of new subsistence objects, as in Robinson Crusoe. Waste, moreover, is also a figure of human activity and existence; it is “the ‘repression’ of this systematic activity of theft and waste of the Earth’s ‘resources.’” 33 As Pagliero observes, via Scanlan: “human history has continually produced waste which, in different ways, is and represents history itself.” 34 Cultures develop as networks of meanings, and waste also possesses its meaning within these cultures. It is not necessary to cite Bataille and his economy of expenditure to understand this. As Viale says: “once thrown away, things—certain things, or even many things—can still be recovered.” 35 Objects, components discarded because they are obsolescent, can well, for example, become the raison d’être of collectors who, thanks to their inventiveness, become true visionary artists: “those who, with the materials collected, engage in tinkering, 30 Simondon, G., 1960–1961, “Psychosociologie de la technicité”, in Sur la technique (1953–1983), J.-Y. Is the Object Obsolescent ? 26 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 including installations and works of art.” 36 This is a way of recognizing the openness of an object to new possible destinations, and even to new social identities. A discarded technical object, a useless component, becomes the engine of artistic invention and can well lead to the production and creation of a work of art or an aesthetic object in general. This type of reuse I will address in the last part of this article, by discussing the case of Rondella, a mysterious artist who sells online his small “peaceful robots” made from real technical waste. For now, let us follow the object “that begins its path toward final disposal.” 37 A whole new way of rethinking the object must be introduced. A new life begins. The privileged place of this new existence of the object is the flea market, where the object awaits a new owner and, hopefully, its new inventor. Flea markets are the cradles of objects to be reused: they can be purchased to continue their existence in other hands, or they can become something else. In any case, this is where the object most often (re)is born. Now, as we know, the object that (re)is born on the stalls of a market can indeed be bought, as mentioned, without changing its function: this is the case when it is purchased by recognizing its structure and functioning. But this way of buying an obsolete object also has a technical character. In most cases, the purchased object is also an object to be repaired. There is an entire culture of tinkering, which Simondon understood. To restore, to repair is above all to learn how to do. The first step toward recovery through restoration is contemplative in nature; it is precisely the expression of that sensitivity toward the object that Simondon spoke of: technical beauty. Contemplation is therefore not separate from knowledge of the object: repairing to reuse is part of (technical) culture. At the base of this culture lies a true love for the object, the same feeling that Fordist culture, in order to justify mass production, emptied of meaning, even erased. Extending the life of an object, as in the case of restoration, means moving from an economy of waste and consumption to a circular economy of recovery, which also has its own way of reinventing objects. It happened to me, while restoring an old phonograph from the 1930s with a friend, that we had to replace missing and irrecoverable parts with elements from other objects, whose function and use we rethought. This was the case with the support arm of the amplifier, which lacked the connector: to repair it, we reused (and rethought) a plastic part from a tube that was used to extend a faucet and diffuse the water flow. In the society of reuse and reinvention, there is no such thing as waste. Everything can serve. This is the principle of ecodesign, that is, design that: “minimizes the presence of toxic substances in products, incorporates recyclable/recycled materials, reduces the quantity and types used, employs materials that are compatible with each other during the recycling phase, reduces the amount of work-related waste, minimizes 36 Viale, G., 2011, La civiltà del riuso. Giovanni Carrozzini 27 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 packaging, uses a reusable packaging system, increases the energy efficiency of electrically powered products, simplifies access to parts for replacement or maintenance, and enables the recovery of components for recycling.” 38 It is from this ecodesign based on durability that the conception and realization of the Phœnix chair, produced by Offecct and designed by Luca Nichetto and Francesco Dompieri, derives. This chair is entirely recoverable; it is an “open” object in Simondon’s sense, that is, “an object that presents itself as fully real, that does not conceal itself.” 39 Easy to assemble, each part of the chair can be recycled once worn out and replaced by new parts which, in turn, can be recycled and replaced: here are the principles of the circular economy at work—an economy that no longer relies on simple linear causality, but on a complex causality that reacts in a controlled way upon itself. Here we find a way of reusing the object that Pagliero summarized as follows: “intervening on an already existing objectual reality by means of operations that could be defined as exogenous because they act on a constructed body defined by structural additions or functional modifications,” 40 which contrasts with the approach that consists in “conceptually defining the structure of any objectual reality to program its possible modifications and changes according to a principle that could be defined as endogenous, or internal, because it is the structure of the object that is modified, according to circumstances, by means of determined transformations.” 41 This is how Nichetto and Dompieri respond to a critical observation by Appiano regarding recycling, which deserves to be quoted in full: “Why don’t large, medium, and small industries think about using less polluting procedures and materials for the production and manufacturing of products, and instead we, the consumers, who have already wasted our money on illusionistic and exaggerated designs and pay taxes for garbage collection, must waste our time subdividing our excessive waste, preparing bulky items, bags of plastic bottles, and others of glass bottles, etc., and go through the endless ritual of unloading one piece at a time into the ‘bells’ for separate collection […]?” 42 Now, when we said that everything is reusable, we did not tell the whole truth: there are, in fact, objects “born to die.” This is the case, among others, with 38 Pulvirenti, E., 2009, Design del riuso. Is the Object Obsolescent ? 28 Aion Journal of Philosophy & Science 3, 2026 batteries; and this is where the reconceptualization of ecodesign comes into play. Batteries are, in fact, objects to be used and thrown away once exhausted. Could new technologies help to rethink them? Moixa Energy Limited thought of solving the problem as follows: “[t]hanks to the USB interface, the battery uses the computer’s current to avoid problems related to the disposal of alkaline batteries or to make the production of elements such as the transformer—necessary for rechargeable batteries—superfluous.” 43 When recycling is no longer possible, we must reinvent! Up to now, the discussion has mainly been about restoring, recycling, and recovering: in other words, about the possible continuation of the life of the object as such, that is, respecting its materials, its structure, its functioning, and its function. To restore, recycle, and recover is to continue the life of the same object. But the true technical gesture toward the worn object, the obsolescent object, consists in reinventing it, or even reusing it—that is, in making one object into another object. 4. Saving the Technical Object: Reuse. Reuse is a transitional practice, to use Pascal Chabot’s expression. 44 But to trans-ire, to go through and beyond, one must first invent—that is, in-venire, to go inside.
